title: Beyond generalizations: Understanding adolescent social networks in American Indian communities
content:
by Shuwen Zhang, Michael D. Siciliano, Nancy Rumbaugh Whitesell, Katie Schultz, Jerreed D. Ivanich

American Indian (AI) adolescents experience disproportionately high rates of substance use, yet the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied. Most existing research on adolescent networks derives from racially heterogeneous school settings, where substance use is often linked to friendship formation and popularity. This study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents in their unique cultural context. Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties. Models assessed endogenous structural processes (reciprocity, transitivity, degree effects) and actor-level characteristics, including demographic factors, substance use (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), depression, and AI identity. Results indicated that universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation) were primary drivers of friendship. However, unlike what is often observed in studies of other adolescent populations, substance use showed no consistent association with sending ties or receiving ties. Similarly, depression and AI identity were not substantively associated with friendship formation. These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors. These findings challenge assumptions underpinning many network-based prevention programs and underscore the critical need for theories and interventions that are culturally and contextually grounded in the lived experiences of AI youth.
author: Shuwen Zhang
